slides.title: Serving concurrently creates budgets before it creates speed
keyPoints: Each connection owns state and consumes resources
Threads share process memory
Admission must bound accepted work
slides.narration: A thread per connection makes a blocking conversation easy to follow, but it does not make resources unlimited. Each admitted client may need a descriptor, stack reservation, request buffer, output buffer, and access to shared services. Those threads share the process's memory, so a cache or counter remains shared even if each thread has its own request object. Start by writing a budget and naming the resource that enforces it. A listening backlog does not cap active clients or worker memory. Concurrency is useful only when the accepted workload can make progress without overwhelming these shared limits.

slides.title: Two separate checks can oversubscribe one remaining slot
keyPoints: Both arrivals observe the same spare capacity
Later increments accept too much work
This is a serialized interleaving model, not a C++ data race
slides.narration: The gate has capacity two and already holds one client. We model two arrivals by making both decisions before either increment. Each sees one active client and says yes. Applying both approvals increases active to three, violating the cap. This program is deliberately single-threaded and contains no data race; it models the logical interleaving of an incorrectly split check and update. A real unsynchronized shared integer would additionally have undefined behavior in C++. Protecting each increment alone is insufficient. The capacity check and the reservation must be one critical section so later arrivals see the earlier reservation.

question.prompt: Why can individually synchronized reads and increments still violate the admission cap?
question.answer: The combined check-and-reserve operation must be atomic with respect to other arrivals. Separating the steps permits both to approve the same remaining slot.

slides.title: An admitted request needs one release on every exit
keyPoints: A permit represents successful admission
Its destructor returns the slot
Exception cleanup can make capacity reusable
slides.narration: This complete example adds lifetime management to a mutex-protected gate. Permit asks the gate to reserve a slot and remembers whether it succeeded. When the scope ends, its destructor releases only a slot it actually owns. The request body deliberately throws after admission. Stack unwinding destroys the permit, and the catch reports the failure. A second permit can then acquire the same capacity, so the output ends with reusable equals one. The permit is not copied because two copied owners could release one reservation twice. This mechanism bounds admitted work; it does not automatically bound every buffer or downstream request.

slides.title: Use the smallest applicable resource ceiling
keyPoints: Descriptors and memory impose separate limits
Reserve headroom for non-client work
Treat stack reservation and resident memory separately
slides.narration: Suppose descriptor accounting permits nine hundred sixty clients, while a memory model permits thirteen hundred sixty-five. The arithmetic ceiling is the smaller number, not their average. The source then chooses an operational cap of two hundred fifty-six to preserve headroom. Those numbers are modeled assumptions, not measurements of this machine. A thread's reserved virtual stack is different from currently resident physical pages, and kernel socket buffers may sit outside a simple application-memory estimate. A defensible budget lists what it includes, what it omits, and which measured workload could force a lower limit.

slides.title: Thread-per-connection
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A thread-per-connection design assigns a worker to each accepted client.
Blocking I/O becomes straightforward because one slow connection blocks its own worker rather than the entire server loop.
The control flow resembles a sequential protocol handler.
The cost grows with active connections: thread stacks, scheduler state, per-connection buffers, and synchronization overhead accumulate.
slides.narration:

An unbounded thread-per-connection loop can exhaust resources before useful work completes. Bound admission and ensure every thread is joined or otherwise owned through shutdown.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Exhaustion occurs when demand exceeds a resource limit.
Symptoms include failed thread creation, descriptor exhaustion, allocation failure, long queues, and timeout cascades.
Rejecting or deferring work deliberately is often safer than accepting everything and failing unpredictably later.
A robust policy specifies admission limits, maximum frame sizes, idle and whole-request deadlines, output-buffer limits, and shutdown behavior.

slides.title: Derive an admission budget
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Assume a hypothetical service budget , not a measurement of the host system:
The descriptor bound is 1024 - 64 = 960 clients when each client uses one descriptor.
The modeled per-client memory is 72 KiB.
The remaining memory is 96 MiB, which permits floor(96 × 1024 / 72) = 1365 clients under those assumptions.
slides.narration: Assume a hypothetical service budget , not a measurement of the host system: The descriptor bound is 1024 - 64 = 960 clients when each client uses one descriptor. The modeled per-client memory is 72 KiB. The remaining memory is 96 MiB, which permits floor(96 × 1024 / 72) = 1365 clients under those assumptions. The combined arithmetic ceiling is therefore 960. Choosing an operational cap of 256 leaves headroom. Its modeled client memory is 256 × 72 KiB = 18 MiB ; adding the 32-MiB base gives 50 MiB. This does not include every possible kernel buffer or thread reservation. The assumptions must be replaced with measurements and explicit accounting before using the number as a deployment limit. Companion listing: ch52/budget.py The output is ceiling=960 cap=256 modeled_MiB=50 . The code verifies the budget calculation, not a claim that 960 live threads or clients are safe on the current machine. Real thread stack reservation and committed use are distinct quantities, and downstream capacity may impose a much lower cap.

slides.title: Per-connection state should stay with its connection
keyPoints: Partial input and pending output are not global scratch space
One owner closes the descriptor
Borrowed access must finish before closure
slides.narration: Two clients can each have half of a header buffered at the same time. Putting both fragments into one global scratch buffer mixes unrelated conversations even if individual writes are locked. Keep framing state, output offsets, deadline information, and the descriptor together in a connection object. That object needs a clear owner, while callbacks and workers may borrow it under a lifetime rule. Closing a descriptor from another thread is not a universal cancellation mechanism, and the integer may later be reused. A stale callback that recognizes only the integer can act on the wrong connection after reuse.

question.prompt: Why does protecting one global request buffer with a mutex still leave a design problem?
question.answer: The buffer does not represent separate in-progress protocols for separate clients. Mutual exclusion alone does not give each connection its own state.

slides.title: Choose a lock boundary around a complete shared operation
keyPoints: Cache lookup plus insertion may be one logical action
Do not hold a global lock across slow client I/O
A copied or owned result can outlive the lock safely
slides.narration: A server cache often needs a compound operation: find a key, decide whether it exists, and possibly install a value. Locking only individual map methods can leave a gap between the decision and the update. Conversely, holding one global lock while writing a slow client's response blocks unrelated clients. A useful design protects the shared data operation, obtains a result with a clear lifetime, and releases the lock before slow I/O when the contract allows it. Returning a borrowed reference into a cache that another thread can erase requires more than simply unlocking quickly.

slides.title: Backpressure is a policy, not a full queue accident
keyPoints: Reject, wait, or shed work deliberately
Bound the waiting queue as well as active clients
Report overload separately from malformed input
slides.narration: When capacity is full, the server must choose what the next request experiences. It can reject promptly, wait within a bounded queue, or apply a documented shedding policy. An unlimited waiting queue only moves resource exhaustion from active workers to queued requests. A bounded queue also needs a waiting deadline or cancellation rule when clients disappear. Distinguish overload from a bad request so callers can respond appropriately, but do not encourage unbounded immediate retries. Admission, queueing, execution, and response delivery are separate stages; each should have a budget and an owner for abandoned work.

slides.title: Creation failure is part of concurrency setup
keyPoints: Some workers may exist when a later creation fails
Track acquired resources as setup progresses
Stop and collect existing workers before shared state dies
slides.narration: Imagine that a server successfully starts three workers but fails to create the fourth. Returning immediately can leave the first three using queues or buffers that are being destroyed. Setup is therefore a sequence of resource acquisitions, not an all-or-nothing magic operation. Record each successful creation, publish shutdown if setup cannot continue, and collect the workers already created before destroying their shared state. Scope-based thread owners can help, but their joins must not wait on work that will never be signaled. The shutdown protocol and lifetime order need to be designed together.

keyPoints: Never exceed the configured active count
Reuse a released slot
Reject without leaking a descriptor or permit
Check zero capacity explicitly
slides.narration: A good gate test checks more than one happy admission. Fill the budget, verify the next request is rejected, release one permit, and verify reuse. Test a zero limit and error paths after successful admission. For actual concurrent tests, collect results after joining and verify the maximum protected active count never exceeded the limit. Do not infer correctness only because one run happened to finish. The logical split-check model shows why the invariant must be justified by the critical section. Leak checks and shutdown tests then cover lifetime obligations that the count alone cannot prove.

slides.title: Choose the server architecture from the workload
keyPoints: Thread per connection favors simple blocking flows
A worker pool bounds executing tasks
An event loop can manage many mostly idle connections
slides.narration: A few long, simple conversations may justify one thread each. A bounded worker pool fits tasks that can be handed off without leaving a thread attached to every idle client. An event loop can service many connections by acting when I/O is ready, but requires explicit partial-operation state. None eliminates framing, ownership, resource bounds, or shutdown. Compare the number of active versus idle clients, work per request, downstream limits, and implementation complexity. The next chapter changes how waiting is organized; it does not remove the shared-resource contracts established here.
